This page gives the statistical framework shared by the Bayesian linear
regression (BLR) models in `sblr`. It defines the core regression models, the
main variance and covariance quantities, and the distinction between the prior
family and the likelihood/operator representation. Detailed derivations for
summary statistics, sample overlap, LD operators, annotation-informed priors,
and multi-trait state spaces are kept on dedicated Methods pages.

## Single-trait regression

For a centered phenotype $y\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$, genotype matrix
$X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}$, marker-effect vector
$b\in\mathbb{R}^{M}$, and observation-level residual vector
$e\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$,

$$
y = Xb + e,
\qquad
e \sim N(0,v_e I_N).
$$

The fitted genetic values are

$$
g = Xb.
$$

Three variance quantities occur repeatedly:

- $v_b$ is the global prior variance scale for an active marker effect;
- $v_g$ is the variance of the combined fitted genetic values $g=Xb$;
- $v_e$ is the residual variance in the observation likelihood.

These have different roles. In particular, $v_b$ belongs to the marker-effect
prior, whereas $v_g$ is induced jointly by the marker effects and genotype
covariance structure. They therefore need not be numerically equal.

For centered genotypes and one common sample, a natural sample-scaled genomic
variance is

$$
\widehat v_g
=
\frac{1}{N}g^\top g
=
\frac{1}{N}b^\top X^\top Xb.
$$

When $\operatorname{Cov}(g,e)=0$, the usual decomposition is

$$
v_y=v_g+v_e,
\qquad
h^2=\frac{v_g}{v_g+v_e}.
$$

A supplied `h2` value used for prior calibration or initialization should not
be confused with a posterior estimate of this ratio.

### BayesC

BayesC uses a point mass at zero and one non-null normal distribution. Let
$d_j\in\{0,1\}$ denote whether marker $j$ is active:

$$
d_j\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_j).
$$

Conditional on the activity state,

$$
b_j=0
\quad\text{if }d_j=0,
$$

and

$$
b_j\mid d_j=1
\sim
N(0,v_bq_j).
$$

The quantity $\pi_j$ controls the prior probability that marker $j$ is active,
whereas $q_j>0$ is a marker-specific relative variance multiplier for an active
effect. In ordinary BayesC,

$$
\pi_j=\pi,
\qquad
q_j=1.
$$

Structured priors may make either quantity marker specific without changing the
Gaussian regression likelihood. The distinction is scientific as well as
computational: $\pi_j$ changes prior activity odds, whereas $q_j$ changes
effect magnitude and shrinkage conditional on activity. Their roles in the
marker conditional are derived in
[Annotation-Informed Priors](annotation_priors.qmd).

### BayesR

BayesR replaces the single non-null distribution with a finite mixture. Let

$$
c_j\in\{0,1,\ldots,K\}
$$

denote the mixture component for marker $j$, with

$$
\gamma_0=0,
\qquad
\gamma_k>0,\quad k=1,\ldots,K.
$$

Write the marker-specific prior component probabilities as

$$
\Pr(c_j=k)=P_{jk},
\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{K}P_{jk}=1.
$$

Then

$$
b_j=0
\quad\text{if }c_j=0,
$$

whereas for a positive component,

$$
b_j\mid c_j=k>0
\sim
N(0,\gamma_kq_jv_b).
$$

The three scale terms have different meanings:

- $\gamma_k$ is the fixed relative variance of BayesR component $k$;
- $q_j$ is a marker-specific relative variance multiplier;
- $v_b$ is the global active-effect variance scale.

Thus, the BayesR component ladder $\gamma_k$ and marker-specific architecture
$q_j$ are not interchangeable. In current R inputs, `mixture_var[1]` is the
null multiplier and corresponds to theoretical component $k=0$.

BayesRC/SBayesRC retains the BayesR effect mixture but makes the marker
component probabilities $P_{jk}$ annotation dependent. Log-variance models
instead retain global probability architecture and learn $q_j$ from
annotations. See [Annotation-Informed Priors](annotation_priors.qmd).

### Posterior marker quantities

Prior probabilities should not be confused with posterior marker summaries.

For BayesC,

$$
\operatorname{PIP}_j
=
\Pr(d_j=1\mid\text{data}).
$$

For BayesR or BayesRC,

$$
\operatorname{PIP}_j
=
1-\Pr(c_j=0\mid\text{data})
=
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Pr(c_j=k\mid\text{data}).
$$

The full posterior component-probability vector contains more information than
the PIP because it also describes uncertainty among positive components. A
final component state is different again: it is one sampled MCMC state, not a
posterior probability vector.

The posterior mean effect,

$$
\mathbb{E}(b_j\mid\text{data}),
$$

is also distinct. Model averaging and sign uncertainty can make it small even
when the PIP is appreciable. Consequently, ranking by PIP and ranking by
absolute posterior mean effect can give different orders.

See [Fine-Mapping and Credible Sets](fine_mapping.qmd) for the relation among
marginal PIPs, posterior configurations, LD, and credible-set post-processing.

## Multi-trait regression

For $T$ traits, collect phenotypes, marker effects, and observation-level
residuals in matrices:

$$
Y=XB+E_Y,
$$

where

$$
Y\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times T},
\qquad
B\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times T},
\qquad
E_Y\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times T}.
$$

Here $B$ is the marker-effect matrix and $E_Y$ is the residual-observation
matrix; neither symbol denotes a covariance matrix. The $j$th row of $B$
contains the effects of marker $j$ across traits. Write the corresponding
trait-effect vector as

$$
\beta_j=B_{j\cdot}^{\top}.
$$

The package-wide theoretical convention is lowercase $v$ for scalar variances
and uppercase $V$ for covariance matrices:

| Quantity | Single trait | Multi trait |
|---|---:|---:|
| active marker effects | $v_b$ | $V_b$ |
| genomic values | $v_g$ | $V_g$ |
| residuals | $v_e$ | $V_e$ |

The matrix of fitted genetic values is

$$
G_X=XB.
$$

For centered genotypes and one common sample,

$$
\widehat V_g
=
\frac{1}{N}G_X^\top G_X
=
\frac{1}{N}B^\top X^\top XB.
$$

This makes the distinction between $V_b$ and $V_g$ explicit: $V_b$ is the
covariance scale in the prior for active marker effects, whereas $V_g$ is
induced by the complete fitted marker-effect matrix and genotype covariance.
Similarly, $V_e$ describes residual covariance across traits.

With summary statistics, inference on $V_e$ requires compatible cross-trait
phenotype products and sample-overlap information; see
[Multi-Trait Sample Overlap](multitrait_overlap.qmd).

### Multi-trait effect covariance

Suppose marker $j$ is assigned to a non-null trait-activity pattern $p$ and a
positive BayesR component $k>0$. Let $V_{b,p}$ denote the active-trait
submatrix of $V_b$. With one marker-specific multiplier shared across traits,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\beta_{j,p,k})
=
\gamma_kq_jV_{b,p}.
$$

The scalar $q_j$ rescales the complete active covariance matrix and therefore
does not by itself change the cross-trait correlation structure encoded by
$V_b$. This shared-$q$ equation is also the mathematical target for a future
MT log-variance extension; it is not a claim that MT-LV is currently
implemented.

### Current multi-trait state probabilities

The current probability model depends on the core family.

Ordinary MT BayesR/SBayesR uses one full `joint_pi` simplex over one unique null
state and all non-null trait-pattern by positive-component combinations.
Component probabilities and trait-pattern probabilities reported from this
model are marginals of the joint simplex; they are not parameters of an
independent $P\times H$ factorization.

Current MT BayesRC/SBayesRC instead factorizes marker component probability and
conditional non-null trait sharing:

$$
\Pr(c_j=0\mid A_j)=P_{j0},
$$

and for $k>0$,

$$
\Pr(a_j=p,c_j=k\mid A_j)
=
P_{jk}H_p.
$$

Here $P_{jk}$ is the marker-specific component architecture and $H_p$ is the
global conditional probability of non-null trait pattern $p$, with

$$
P_{j0}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}P_{jk}=1,
\qquad
\sum_pH_p=1.
$$

Current MT BayesRC annotations therefore change $P$, not $H$, and do not make
$V_b$ annotation dependent. See
[MT BayesR/SBayesR](mt_bayesr_sbayesr.qmd) and
[MT BayesRC/SBayesRC](mt_bayesrc_sbayesrc.qmd).

## Prior family versus likelihood representation

The prior family and likelihood representation are separate parts of the
model. Schematically, if $\Theta$ denotes all unknown model states,

$$
p(\Theta\mid\text{data})
\propto
L_{\mathrm{operator}}(\text{data}\mid\Theta)
\,p_{\mathrm{prior}}(\Theta).
$$

For single-trait Gaussian regression, the relevant cross-products are

$$
X^\top y,
\qquad
X^\top X,
\qquad
y^\top y.
$$

Throughout the Methods documentation, these mathematical cross-products are
written explicitly rather than using implementation field names as mathematical
symbols. In the current `sblr` interfaces, $X^\top y$ is commonly stored as
`wy`, the diagonal of $X^\top X$ is stored as `ww` where applicable, and
$y^\top y$ is stored as `yy`. Some multi-trait/native interfaces use `Xy` for
the corresponding matrix $X^\top Y$. These are code conventions rather than
distinct statistical quantities.

Up to terms not depending on $b$, the single-trait Gaussian log likelihood is

$$
\log L(y\mid b,v_e)
=
-\frac{1}{2v_e}
\left(
y^\top y
-2b^\top X^\top y
+b^\top X^\top Xb
\right)
+\text{constant}.
$$

This identity explains why summary-statistic BLR can operate on cross-products.
It also shows why the LD/operator representation matters: different operators
provide different representations or approximations to the genotype
cross-product information entering the likelihood.

Current routes include:

- packed BED, using selected individual-level genotypes;
- CSR sparse LD, combining summary cross-products with sparse off-diagonal LD;
- block eigen, using within-block spectral representations, including the
  retained-factor form for current scalar fits and reconstructed dense blocks
  where supported.

Different operator approximations can therefore produce different posterior
marker effects and PIPs even when the prior family is the same. For details,
see [Summary Statistics](summary_statistics.qmd),
[Sparse-LD CSR](sparse_ld_csr.qmd), and
[Block-Eigen LD](block_eigen_operator.qmd).

## The `S` prefix and MAF-S are different concepts

The `S` prefix in SBayesC, SBayesR, and SBayesRC identifies the
summary-statistics model/likelihood context. It does not define a different
effect prior by itself and it is not the BayesS-style MAF parameter.

MAF-dependent prior scaling is controlled separately by `maf_effect_s`. Thus:

- BayesR and SBayesR share the same core finite-mixture prior family;
- the summary-statistics route changes how likelihood information is supplied;
- MAF-S, when enabled, changes marker-specific prior effect variance.

The relationship between MAF-S and the general variance architecture $q_j$ is
described in [Annotation-Informed Priors](annotation_priors.qmd).
